# Abstract

Although there is consensus that human impacts have shaped ecosystems and biodiversity for millennia, the relative roles of climate and human activity in affecting the structure of Holocene ecosystems remain poorly understood. There has been no systematic global attempt to determine the relative strength of these two drivers at regional to continental scales using multiple properties of fossil pollen assemblages. Here, we integrate palaeoecological, archaeological, and palaeoclimate data to quantify the relative importance of climate and human activity in shaping pollen assemblage dynamics from 8.5 to 2.0 ka BP. The preparation and expert-screening pool contained `r format(preparation_pool_n, big.mark = ",")` fossil pollen records, of which `r format(original_h1_inventory_n, big.mark = ",")` entered the original H1 model inventory. We examined ten pollen assemblage properties (PAPs), including the added $N_1-N_2$ metric, and assessed how relationships among PAPs changed during the study interval. We combined archaeological radiocarbon SPDs and complementary expert-screened event chronologies with palaeoclimate-model output, while controlling time within records and spatial structure among records. Climate exceeded human influence in `r format(spatial_climate_dominant_n, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(spatial_controlled_n, big.mark = ",")` controlled spatial records (`r sprintf("%.1f", spatial_climate_dominant_pct)`%) and in `r temporal_climate_dominant_n` of `r temporal_spd_n` estimable regional time slices. Signed and alternative HVarPart profiles retained the same broad ordering, although proxy, radius, and dependence sensitivities altered some individual estimates. Our results support climate as the predominant correlate of continental and subcontinental pollen assemblage dynamics during the Middle and Late Holocene, while neither excluding consequential human effects at finer spatial scales nor supporting taxon-specific inference.
